article.title: Chattel Slavery vs. Wage Labor: Who Is Really Free?
article.author: Sharon Kyle
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In 1860, nearly four million Black people were enslaved in the United States. Their labor produced enormous wealth, but they had virtually no control over what they made or who benefited from it. They planted and harvested cotton, cultivated tobacco and sugar, built homes, maintained households, and practiced skilled trades. Today, American workers produce goods and services on a scale unimaginable in 1860. Yet millions struggle to afford housing, healthcare, education, childcare, food, and retirement. The question connecting these eras is not whether the systems are the same. They are profoundly different. It is this: Who controls the wealth people create, and who is really free? Two Systems, Different Forms of Power Under chattel slavery, people were legally treated as property. They could be bought, sold, separated from their families, and subjected to violence. They could not freely leave or negotiate the terms of their labor. Wage workers, by contrast, are legally free. In theory, they can change employers, negotiate pay, organize unions, own property, and exercise political rights. Those freedoms matter. But legal freedom does not guarantee economic independence. People with little access to land, capital, or other sources of income generally have to sell their labor to survive. When necessities depend on a paycheck, refusing unfavorable work can be difficult. Critics have called this condition wage slavery . The phrase should not erase the violence and total denial of personhood at the heart of chattel slavery. It points instead to a question about economic power: How much control can people exercise over their lives when they depend on owners and employers for access to work and income? The 1860 Debate—and the Civil War By 1860, slavery and wage labor were expanding in different parts of the country. Southern enslavers defended an economy built on forced Black labor. In the North, factories, railroads, commercial agriculture, and wage employment were growing. The fight to expand slavery—and the political power of enslavers—helped drive the nation toward civil war. The conflict was not a balanced contest between two equivalent labor systems; slavery was central to secession and the war that followed. www.nps.gov Still, people at the time debated the insecurity of wage labor. Proslavery writer George Fitzhugh argued that Northern employers treated workers more cruelly than enslavers treated people they held in bondage. He claimed enslavers had a paternalistic duty to provide for them, while employers could dismiss workers when they were no longer profitable. Fitzhugh was not calling for workers’ liberation. He used the risks of wage dependence to defend human bondage, while ignoring slavery’s violence, family separation, sexual exploitation, and denial of personhood. His argument nevertheless shows that the unequal power between employers and workers was already a subject of public debate. Abraham Lincoln imagined a different possibility. In an 1859 address, he described wage work as a stage from which a person might earn, save, acquire tools or land, and eventually work independently. His vision assumed workers could move beyond dependence on wages. abrahamlincolnonline.org That path was never open to everyone, and it became harder to follow as industrial capitalism grew. But the shift toward wage dependence was not simply inevitable. Worker-owned cooperatives and other forms of shared ownership could have let people produce at scale while retaining collective control over their lives, their work and its rewards. Political choices could have supported those alternatives. Emancipation Without Resources The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery, except as punishment for a crime following conviction. But legal freedom did not return to formerly enslaved people the land, wealth, or authority they had been denied. In Life and Times of Frederick Douglass , Douglass describes formerly enslaved people being turned out of their quarters and left to find food and shelter. He writes that they were “without food, without shelter, without land, without money, and without friends,” and describes them as “naked to the open sky.” en.wikisource.org The episode makes the former enslavers’ sense of ownership starkly visible. Even after emancipation, some acted as though the land and shelter where people had lived—and the resources needed to survive—still belonged to them. Douglass’s account shows how little emancipation alone changed the material power of those who had controlled people’s labor and lives. That history matters to this article because freedom is not only a legal status. It also depends on whether people have the resources and power to make meaningful choices. Wage Labor Won—but It Wasn’t the Only Option Today, paid employment is the predominant way people earn a living. For much of American history, however, people worked on farms, in family enterprises, or in independent trades. As wage employment expanded, more people rented their time and labor to employers, surrendering some control over how their lives and work was organized and who received its proceeds. That transition helped build extraordinary productive capacity in the United States. It also concentrated decision-making into the hands of the elite. In many workplaces, owners and executives determine what gets made, how work is organized, and whether workers keep their jobs. The wealth that is extracted by those businesses is generated by labor. It is a collective effort, but authority over that wealth is often concentrated in relatively few hands. The Collective Makes the Fortune We are often told that hard work guarantees success: work hard, make the right choices, and you will get ahead. But effort alone does not determine who becomes wealthy. Ownership does. Workers make goods and provide services. Consumers create markets by buying them. Families provide care that sustains workers and raises the next generation. Taxpayers support infrastructure, education, research, and public institutions businesses rely on. Great fortunes depend on this broad, collective contribution, even when the returns flow disproportionately to owners and investors. By fall 2026, public estimates had placed Elon Musk’s net worth above $1 trillion, largely reflecting the value of his ownership stakes. Such estimates can change with markets, but the scale points to a larger concern: concentrated wealth can bring concentrated power. businessinsider.com Billionaires—and a person valued at over a trillion dollars—can make decisions that reshape workplaces and livelihoods, including firing large numbers of workers. The criticism is not that owners have no role in building companies. It is that legal ownership can give a few people sweeping authority over enterprises whose success depends on the work of many. Workers can be treated as disposable while the people who control the assets act as though the wealth belongs to them alone. Ordinary people are not to blame for participating. People work, shop, and pay bills within a system where opting out can mean losing access to necessities. The danger is that our essential participation helps build private power over which we have little say—and that power can then shape the conditions under which we live and work. Who Is Really Free? Under chattel slavery, the law assigned control of labor and its proceeds to enslavers. Under contemporary capitalism, much of the power to direct production rests with owners, investors, and executives. Workers can organize; government can regulate and redistribute; cooperatives and public institutions can provide alternatives. Those possibilities depend on political choices. The United States abolished the legal ownership of human beings without ending the concentration of economic power. It developed extraordinary productive capacity without ensuring that everyone shares in its benefits. America can produce enormous wealth. The question is whether the people who produce it will gain enough power to decide what it is for—and who benefits. Emancipation ended the legal ownership of human beings. The struggle for economic democracy asks what freedom requires beyond that.
